analogy.p: Picture a steering wheel with the driver's left hand pushing up on one side and the right hand pulling down on the other side. Two equal and opposite pushes on opposite sides of the centre make the wheel turn, just as the opposite forces on the two sides of a motor coil make it rotate. The commutator is like the driver swapping hands at the top and bottom so that the pushes keep turning the wheel the same way. The analogy breaks down because in a real motor the forces come from a magnetic field acting on a current, not from muscles, and no 'hand-swapping' is needed by a person: the split ring does it automatically.
analogy.t: Two people turning a steering wheel

bullets: The **strength** of the field around a wire **increases** when the **current increases**.
The field is **strongest close to the wire** and gets weaker with **increasing distance** from the wire, so the circles are drawn closer together near the wire.
**Reversing the direction of the current** reverses the direction of the field lines.
Shaping the wire into a **solenoid** (a long coil) adds up the fields of every turn, so the field inside is **strong and uniform** and the pattern outside is the same as that of a **bar magnet**.
A solenoid's field can be made stronger by increasing the current, adding more turns per unit length, or inserting a **soft iron core** (this makes an **electromagnet**).
An electromagnet can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed, which is why electromagnets (not permanent magnets) are used in motors, relays and scrapyard cranes.
**Link to other topics:** the idea that a current produces a field is the reason a magnetic compass is deflected near a live wire.
core.h: The magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
core.p: Whenever there is a **current** in a conductor, a **magnetic field** is produced around it. Close to a long straight wire the field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, lying in planes at right angles to the wire. The field is not made by the wire's material being magnetic: it is made by the moving charges themselves, so it vanishes the instant the current is switched off. This is the foundation of the whole topic, because the motor effect is simply two magnetic fields interacting.

bullets: Newton's third law applies: the magnet exerts a force on the wire and the wire exerts an **equal and opposite force** on the magnet.
If the wire is **parallel** to the magnetic field lines, there is **no force**.
The force is at **right angles to both** the field and the current, never along either of them.
**Reversing the current** reverses the force direction; **reversing the field** (swapping the poles) also reverses it.
Reversing **both** the current and the field leaves the force in the **same direction**.
A force of this type is what makes a **current balance** work and is the basic physics behind every electric motor, loudspeaker and some electric trains.
The force on the wire is zero when there is no current, which is why a motor stops when it is switched off.
core.h: The motor effect: what it is and when it happens
core.p: When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the **magnet producing the field** and the **conductor** exert a **force on each other**. This is called the **motor effect**. The force arises because the field of the magnet and the field around the wire interact: where the two fields point in the same direction they add and where they point oppositely they partly cancel, and the wire is pushed from the strong side towards the weak side. A wire only feels the force if it is **not parallel** to the field lines, and the force is largest when the wire is at **right angles** to the field.

bullets: **Thumb = force (motion), First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current**: the letters spell out what each finger shows.
The field direction is always from **north to south**; current direction is the **conventional current**, from **+ to -**.
Worked idea: field pointing right, current pointing into the page, force points **down** the page (see the diagram).
If the current is reversed, the thumb flips by 180 degrees; if both are reversed, it points the same way.
Use the rule on **each** side of a motor coil separately: the two long sides have currents in opposite directions, so the forces are in **opposite** directions.
In exam answers, state clearly **which finger represents which quantity**; marks are lost for vague 'use the left hand rule'.
The rule gives only the **direction**; the size comes from F = B x I x l.
core.p: **Fleming's left-hand rule** is a way of working out the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Hold the **thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to one another**. The **First finger** points in the direction of the **Field** (from the **N pole to the S pole**), the se**C**ond finger points in the direction of the **Current** (from the **positive to the negative terminal**, conventional current), and the **thuMb** points in the direction of the force or **Motion** of the conductor. You must use the **left** hand, as the right hand would give the opposite direction.

bullets: **Equation:** F = B x I x l, so **B = F / (I x l)**, **I = F / (B x l)** and **l = F / (B x I)**.
**Units:** 1 tesla = 1 newton per ampere per metre (1 N/A/m), but you only need to quote T.
F is **directly proportional** to each of B, I and l: doubling the current doubles the force.
Only the **length of wire actually in the field** counts, so use the length of the wire between the poles, not the whole wire.
The equation applies only when the wire is **at right angles** to the field; at other angles the force is smaller, and parallel gives zero.
Convert **centimetres to metres** before substituting (for example 8 cm = 0.08 m); this is the most common slip.
Typical sizes: a small motor wire in a magnet may feel only a few hundredths of a newton, which is why motors use **many turns** to add up the forces.
core.h: Calculating the force: F = B I l (Higher tier)
core.p: For a conductor **at right angles to a magnetic field** and carrying a current, the size of the force is given by **force = magnetic flux density x current x length**. In symbols **F = B I l**. The force is measured in **newtons (N)**, the flux density **B** in **tesla (T)**, the current **I** in **amperes (A)** and the length **l** of the conductor that is **inside the field** in **metres (m)**. Magnetic flux density is a measure of how strong the magnetic field is, so a stronger magnet or a bigger current gives a bigger force.

bullets: The current in the short sides of the coil is parallel or nearly parallel to the field, so those sides feel little or no useful force.
When the coil is **parallel to the field** the forces act at their largest distance from the axle, so the turning effect is **greatest**.

When the coil reaches the **vertical position** (its plane at right angles to the field), the forces on the two sides act **along the line of the coil**, so there is **no turning effect** at that instant.
The coil's **momentum** carries it through the vertical position, where the commutator then swaps the current direction.
The energy transfer is **electrical energy to kinetic energy**, with some wasted as **heat** because of the resistance of the coil and friction at the brushes.
Real motors use **many turns** of wire, a **soft iron core** and **curved pole pieces** to give a stronger, steadier turning effect.
Opposite forces on opposite sides is the key mark-scheme idea: always say **'the current is in opposite directions on the two sides, so the forces are in opposite directions'**.
core.h: How the motor effect makes a coil rotate: the d.c. electric motor (Higher tier)
core.p: A **coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate**, and this is the basis of the **electric motor**. In a simple d.c. motor a rectangular coil lies between the north and south poles of a permanent magnet. The current runs **up one side of the coil and back down the other**, so the current in the two long sides is in **opposite directions**. By Fleming's left-hand rule the forces on these two sides are therefore **opposite**: one side is pushed up and the other is pushed down. Two equal and opposite forces acting on opposite sides of the axle produce a **turning effect** (a moment), which makes the coil spin about its axle.

bullets: The commutator **reverses the direction of the current** in the coil **every half turn**.
The brushes are made of **carbon** because it conducts, is slippery (low friction) and is soft so it does not wear the metal ring too quickly.
The gaps in the split ring line up with the brushes at the **vertical position**, where the current momentarily stops.
Without the commutator, the coil would **flip back and forth** and stop.
The motor is called a **d.c. motor** because it is supplied by direct current, but the current **in the coil** alternates in direction.
If the battery is reversed, the forces reverse and the coil spins the **opposite** way.
A common mark-scheme phrase: **'the split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn so the coil continues to rotate in the same direction'**.
core.p: If the current in the coil stayed the same, the coil would turn only to the vertical position and then be pulled back, oscillating instead of spinning. The **split-ring commutator** solves this. It is a ring cut into two halves, each joined to one end of the coil, and it rotates with the coil. **Carbon brushes** press lightly against it and connect it to the battery. Every **half turn** each half of the ring moves from one brush to the other, so the **current in the coil is reversed**. That means the side of the coil now on the left (which was being pushed up) is carrying current in the opposite direction, so it is still pushed in the **same rotational direction**, and the coil keeps spinning one way.

bullets: **Increase the current** (a higher potential difference or lower resistance) to increase F and the speed.
Use a **stronger magnet** (or stronger magnetic field) to increase B.
Use **more turns of wire** on the coil so that there are more current-carrying sides in the field.
Use a **longer coil** (more wire in the field) or add a **soft iron core** to strengthen the field.
**Reverse the battery connections** or **swap the magnet's poles** to reverse the direction of rotation.
Reversing **both** at the same time keeps the original direction.
A variable resistor in series with the motor changes the current and so changes the speed.
core.h: Changing the speed and direction of a motor
core.p: A designer or an exam question may ask how to make a motor spin **faster** or **in the opposite direction**. Everything follows from F = B I l and the turning effect: increasing any quantity that increases the forces increases the turning effect, so the motor accelerates until the opposing frictional and load forces balance. To reverse the direction you must reverse one, but not both, of the current or the field.

bullets: The **frequency of the sound** equals the **frequency of the alternating current**, so a higher-pitched note is a faster alternating current.
The **amplitude** (loudness) of the sound depends on the **size of the current**: a larger current gives a larger force and bigger vibrations.
The cone is **large and light** so that it pushes a lot of air without having much inertia.
**Headphones** work in the same way but are smaller, with the cone (diaphragm) close to the ear.
Energy transfer: **electrical energy to kinetic energy to sound energy**.
The loudspeaker is the **reverse** of a microphone: a loudspeaker turns electrical signals into sound, a microphone turns sound into electrical signals (generator effect).
This content is labelled **Physics only** in the AQA specification, so check if your course covers it; the motor effect behind it is needed for all.
core.p: A **moving-coil loudspeaker** is the motor effect used to turn an **electrical signal into sound**. A **permanent magnet** is fixed in the speaker, and a **coil of wire** (the voice coil) fits around or inside it and is attached to a **paper or plastic cone**. The **alternating current** from the amplifier flows through the coil and, because the coil is in the magnet's field, it experiences a **force**. As the current alternates, the **force alternates in direction**, so the coil, and the cone attached to it, **move backwards and forwards** (vibrate). The cone pushes the air, producing **compressions and rarefactions**, which travel away as a **sound wave**.

bullets: Step 1: **mark the field direction** with an arrow from the N pole to the S pole.
Step 2: **mark the current direction** from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
Step 3: hold your **left hand** so that the first finger points along the field and the second along the current.
Step 4: the **thumb** gives the force direction; write it relative to the page or the labelled poles.
Check by reversing one quantity: the force must flip.
If asked about a **coil**, repeat for each long side and explain that the forces are opposite.
If the wire is parallel to the field, state that there is **no force**.
core.h: Worked method for motor-effect direction questions
core.p: Direction questions are among the most reliably tested parts of this topic, and they are quick marks if you have a routine. First decide which direction is the field (always from N to S). Next decide which direction is the current (from + to - in the wire, or from your circuit diagram). Then use your left hand to find the force. Finally describe the result in a sentence that names the direction relative to the diagram, such as 'upwards, towards the top of the page'.

bullets: Motor effect: **input is electrical, output is movement**; used in motors, loudspeakers, headphones.
Generator effect: **input is movement, output is electrical**; used in dynamos, alternators, microphones.
Fleming's **left-hand** rule is for the **motor** effect; the generator effect has the opposite action but is not tested with a hand rule at GCSE.
Both rely on a **conductor** and a **magnetic field** and on them being at an angle to each other.
An actual motor, when spun by hand, acts as a **generator**, which is how regenerative braking recovers energy.
In a motor, the induced pd from the generator effect partly **opposes** the supply pd as the coil spins (a 'back pd').
core.h: Comparing the motor effect with the generator effect
core.p: Students often confuse these two. In the **motor effect** a **current in a magnetic field produces a force** (electrical energy is transferred into movement). In the **generator effect** a **conductor moving in a magnetic field produces a potential difference** (movement is transferred into electrical energy). They are opposite processes and many devices (like a loudspeaker and a microphone) are matched pairs using each.

bullets: **Energy:** useful output = kinetic energy of the motor and load; wasted energy = heat from resistance and friction.
**Electricity:** a variable resistor or a change in the supply pd changes the current and so the speed.
**Forces:** two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action are different produce a **moment** (turning effect).
**Waves:** the cone makes a **longitudinal** wave whose frequency matches the alternating current.
**Everyday uses:** washing machines, fans, electric cars, hard disk drives, trains and speakers.
**Magnetism:** a stronger magnet or electromagnet increases the force, as the field B increases.
**Practical idea:** you can investigate how the force on a wire depends on the current by measuring the apparent mass change on a balance.
core.h: Link to other topics and common contexts
core.p: The motor effect links the electricity, magnetism and energy topics. In electricity, the current and the length in F = B I l tie into charge flow and potential difference. In energy, motors transfer **electrical energy to kinetic energy** and you can be asked to calculate efficiency. In forces, a turning effect is a **moment**, and in waves a loudspeaker produces **longitudinal sound waves**. Being able to link these ideas is how you reach the top marks in 6-mark questions.

exam: **Command words:** 'State' needs a short fact (such as 'left hand'); 'Describe' needs what happens; 'Explain' needs the reason using 'because' or 'so'.
**1 mark:** recall such as the unit of magnetic flux density (tesla) or what the commutator does.
**2 marks:** F = B I l calculations: one mark for substitution, one for the answer with unit; or a pair of linked statements.
**3 marks:** typically a short explanation: 'current in opposite directions on the two sides, so forces opposite, so coil rotates'.
**4 marks:** describe how a motor works, including a diagram reference: field, current, forces, turning effect.
**6 marks:** explain the motor and how to make it faster or reverse it; structure as: how it rotates, role of commutator, then changes with reasons.
**Model phrases:** 'a force acts on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field', 'the forces are in opposite directions', 'the commutator reverses the current every half turn'.
**Equation:** learn **F = B I l** and its rearrangements (B = F / Il, I = F / Bl, l = F / BI) and practise all three.
**Convert units** before substituting: cm to m and mA to A.
**Direction questions:** name the finger for each quantity; marks for the final direction depend on it.
**Always give units** (N, T, A, m) and a sensible number of significant figures.
**Loudspeaker answers:** mention alternating current, alternating force, vibrating cone and sound waves for four marks.

mistakes.r: The force is at right angles to both the field and the current.
mistakes.w: The force is in the direction of the magnetic field or the current.

mistakes.r: Use the left hand (for the motor effect).
mistakes.w: Use the right hand for Fleming's rule.

mistakes.r: The force arises from the interaction of the two magnetic fields; it is perpendicular to the field, not towards a pole.
mistakes.w: The wire is attracted to one pole of the magnet.

mistakes.r: The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn; the supply is d.c.
mistakes.w: The commutator makes the current alternate in the supply.

mistakes.r: The two sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions, so forces on them are opposite and give a turning effect.
mistakes.w: The coil turns because the magnet attracts it.

mistakes.r: Convert to metres (0.08 m) before substituting.
mistakes.w: Using 8 cm directly in F = B I l.

mistakes.r: The force is greatest at right angles to the field and zero if the wire is parallel to it.
mistakes.w: Putting the wire parallel to the field to get the biggest force.

mistakes.r: A stronger magnet increases B, so the force increases; the current is set by the supply and resistance.
mistakes.w: A stronger magnet makes the current larger.

mistakes.r: The alternating current in the coil causes alternating forces so the coil and cone vibrate, pushing the air.
mistakes.w: A loudspeaker makes sound by the cone being magnetic.

summary: The spec requires you to know that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (the motor effect), to use Fleming's left-hand rule and F = B I l (Higher), and to explain how this makes a d.c. motor, with a split-ring commutator, and a loudspeaker work. It matters because the motor effect is the basis of almost every machine that converts electrical energy into movement.

terms.d: When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet and the conductor exert a force on each other.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
The unit of magnetic flux density.
A long coil of wire that, when carrying a current, produces a strong, uniform magnetic field inside it.
A solenoid with a soft iron core that is magnetised only while a current flows.
A rule linking the directions of the field (first finger), current (second finger) and force or motion (thumb) for a conductor in a magnetic field.
A rotating ring in two halves that reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that the coil keeps spinning in the same direction.
A carbon contact that presses against the commutator and carries current to and from the coil.
The tendency of a force to cause rotation about a pivot, given by force x perpendicular distance.
Current direction taken from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole; from N to S outside a magnet.
Current that repeatedly changes direction, with a frequency in hertz.
A device using the motor effect to make a cone vibrate and so convert electrical signals into sound.
The coil attached to a loudspeaker cone.
A core of easily magnetised and demagnetised iron that strengthens the field of a coil.

worked.q: A straight wire of length 0.080 m carries a current of 5.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire. [2 marks]
steps: Write the equation: F = B x I x l.

worked.q: The wire in a magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T is 12 cm long and experiences a force of 0.36 N. Calculate the current. [3 marks]

worked.ans: The alternating current in the coil, which is in a magnetic field, causes a force on it (motor effect). As the current reverses, the force reverses direction, so the coil and cone move backwards and forwards (vibrate) with the same frequency as the current. The vibrating cone makes the air vibrate, producing a sound wave.
worked.q: Explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker produces sound. [4 marks]
steps: Alternating current flows in a coil that is placed in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet.
This causes a force on the coil (motor effect).
The current changes direction so the force changes direction, making the coil and attached cone vibrate.
The cone pushes the air, producing sound waves of the same frequency as the current.
